title: Improving Students’ Learning With Effective Learning Techniques: Promising Directions From Cognitive and Educational Psychology
publication: Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 14(1), 4–58
license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages and DOI matched on scholars.duke.edu (Duke Scholars record) and fds.duke.edu; the utility ratings matched in the eurekalert.org press release and a texasldcenter.org summary.

summary: A long monograph that reviews ten techniques students use to learn and gives each an overall utility rating. Practice testing and distributed practice are rated high; interleaved practice, elaborative interrogation and self-explanation are rated moderate; summarization, highlighting, the keyword mnemonic, imagery for text and rereading are rated low. The striking pattern is that the most popular techniques, rereading and highlighting, are among the weakest.
arguments: Practice testing (retrieving information rather than reviewing it) and distributed practice (spacing study over time) have the broadest support of the ten techniques.
Interleaved practice, elaborative interrogation and self-explanation are promising but rest on a narrower evidence base, so they receive a moderate rating.
Rereading and highlighting feel productive but show low utility for durable learning.
design: Narrative review of experimental and applied research on ten learning techniques, each given an overall utility rating (high, moderate or low).
strengths: Broad, carefully reasoned synthesis by leading cognitive and educational psychologists; explicit about the limits of each technique’s evidence; widely used as a reference in education.
limitations: Ratings are expert judgments rather than pooled effect sizes. The review concerns academic learning (text, facts, concepts, problem solving), not motor skills or workplace performance.
contested: The high ratings for testing and spacing are among the most robust conclusions in applied cognitive psychology. Interleaving’s moderate rating reflects a thinner evidence base at the time; how far these principles transfer to motor skills is a separate question (see R-czyz-2024-effect, R-ammar-2023-myth).
generalizability: High confidence for learning facts, concepts and procedures that must be recalled later, including professional knowledge (rules, protocols, playbooks). Use caution when extending the ratings to motor skills without motor-learning evidence.
relevance: Gives you a defensible evidence ranking for the learning methods your staff and players already use, and a vocabulary for retiring the weakest ones.

title: Test-Enhanced Learning: Taking Memory Tests Improves Long-Term Retention
license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages and DOI matched on pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (PMID 16507066) and profiles.wustl.edu; design and findings matched in the PubMed abstract.

summary: Two experiments in which students read prose passages and then either restudied them or took free-recall tests without feedback. Restudying produced better recall on a test five minutes later, but testing produced better recall after two days and after one week. Students who restudied were more confident they would remember, even though they remembered less.
arguments: Retrieval is not only a way to measure learning; it changes memory and improves long-term retention.
The advantage of testing appears only after a delay; on an immediate test the pattern reverses.
Learners’ confidence tracked the less effective strategy, so self-assessment during study is a poor guide to durable learning.
design: Experiment 1: study a passage, then restudy it or take a recall test; final test after 5 minutes, 2 days or 1 week. Experiment 2: four study periods, three study periods and one test, or one study period and three tests; final test after 5 minutes or 1 week.
strengths: Clean experimental manipulation; delayed tests at several intervals; demonstrates the crossover between immediate performance and later retention that defines the learning–performance distinction.
limitations: University students and prose passages in a laboratory; no feedback was given on tests; retention intervals of up to one week.
generalizability: The testing effect has since been reproduced across many materials and settings (see R-dunlosky-2013-improving). It transfers well to any knowledge that must be retrieved under pressure, such as protocols, scouting information or rules. It is not direct evidence about motor skills.
relevance: The cleanest demonstration that the condition which looks better in the moment can be the one that teaches less, and that learners are fooled by it.

title: Learning Versus Performance: An Integrative Review
license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages and DOI matched on pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (PMID 25910388); scope of the review matched in the PubMed abstract.

summary: An integrative review of research showing that performance during training and long-term learning are different things. Drawing on animal learning, motor learning and verbal learning, the authors show that learning can occur without visible performance gains, that performance gains can fail to produce learning, and that some manipulations move the two in opposite directions. They also review how learners and instructors misread current performance as evidence of learning.
arguments: Learning (a relatively permanent change that supports retention and transfer) must be inferred from delayed or changed-context tests, not from performance during practice.
Conditions that slow acquisition — spacing, variation, interleaving, reduced guidance — can enhance long-term retention and transfer.
Learners and instructors are prone to treating fluent, error-free practice as proof of learning.
design: Narrative integrative review spanning animal learning, motor-skill learning, verbal learning and metacognition.
strengths: Unifies findings from several traditions under one distinction; written by a leading researcher on desirable difficulties; covers both motor and verbal learning.
limitations: Narrative rather than meta-analytic; much of the underlying evidence comes from laboratory tasks with short retention intervals. The review predates recent bias-corrected meta-analyses of some motor-learning effects.
contested: The distinction itself is well established. The size and applied reliability of specific desirable difficulties in motor learning are debated (see R-czyz-2024-effect, R-ammar-2023-myth, R-mckay-2024-reporting).
generalizability: The distinction applies to any training program, in sport, medicine, aviation or business. Effect sizes for particular techniques should not be assumed to carry over from the laboratory.
relevance: The single most useful idea for anyone who evaluates practice: what you see in the session is performance, and learning is what remains later.

title: The Role of Deliberate Practice in the Acquisition of Expert Performance
license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages and DOI matched in the KU Leuven Lirias repository record (lirias.kuleuven.be), scilit.net and the reference list of a 2016 reply by Macnamara and colleagues; the abstract’s ten-year claim matched in a summary of the paper.

summary: The founding statement of deliberate-practice theory. The authors argue that expert performance results from a long period of deliberate practice — effortful activity designed to improve specific aspects of performance — and that many characteristics once attributed to innate talent are the product of intense practice extended over at least ten years. They support the framework with studies in which music students of different skill levels gave retrospective estimates of their accumulated practice.
arguments: Deliberate practice is distinct from play, work and mere repetition: it targets specific weaknesses, is effortful, and relies on feedback and, often, a teacher’s design.
Groups at higher skill levels reported more accumulated deliberate practice.
Expert performance reflects acquired adaptations more than fixed innate capacity.
design: Theoretical framework supported by cross-sectional studies of music students grouped by skill level, using retrospective estimates of accumulated practice.
strengths: Precise definition of a kind of practice; shifted research attention from innate talent to the structure of training; generated decades of research.
limitations: Cross-sectional comparisons of groups already differing in skill; retrospective self-reports of practice over many years; small samples; cannot separate the effect of practice from the possibility that more able or motivated people practice more.
contested: Meta-analyses find practice explains a modest share of performance differences (R-macnamara-2014-deliberate, R-macnamara-2016-relationship), and a replication of the violin study found a smaller effect (R-macnamara-2019-role). Ericsson and colleagues reply that those analyses used a broader definition than deliberate practice (R-ericsson-2019-deliberate).
generalizability: The definition of high-quality practice is useful in sport, music, medicine and professional work. The strong claim that accumulated deliberate practice largely explains individual differences is not well supported outside the original framework.
relevance: You will hear its ideas (and its popular distortions) in every conversation about talent and reps; you need the original to separate the two.

title: Deliberate Practice and Performance in Music, Games, Sports, Education, and Professions: A Meta-Analysis
license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, year, journal and DOI matched on sciencedaily.com (press release) and stafforini.com; domain-by-domain variance figures matched in the press release and a quoted abstract. Volume and pages were not confirmed and are omitted.

summary: A meta-analysis of studies relating amount of deliberate practice to performance across five domains. Practice explained about 26% of performance variance in games, 21% in music, 18% in sports, 4% in education and less than 1% in professions. The authors conclude that deliberate practice is important but not as important as had been argued.
arguments: Accumulated practice is positively related to performance in every domain studied.
The share of performance differences it explains is modest and varies sharply by domain.
Other factors must account for most individual differences in performance, which calls for a multifactorial account of expertise.
design: Meta-analysis of studies reporting both a measure of accumulated practice and a measure of performance, grouped by domain (press coverage reports 88 studies).
strengths: Quantitative synthesis across domains; tests the strong claim of deliberate-practice theory directly; transparent about domain differences.
limitations: Depends on how primary studies measured practice (often retrospective estimates) and performance; critics argue its inclusion criteria captured practice broader than deliberate practice as originally defined.
contested: Ericsson and Harwell argue that studies matching the original definition show larger effects (R-ericsson-2019-deliberate). The authors’ sport-specific follow-up reached similar conclusions (R-macnamara-2016-relationship).
generalizability: Directly relevant to sport and professional development. Variance explained describes differences among people in a sample, not how much any one person can improve with practice.
relevance: The central counterweight to the belief that more hours reliably produce experts; essential for any talent or development investment.

title: The Relationship Between Deliberate Practice and Performance in Sports: A Meta-Analysis
license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages and DOI matched in an author copy hosted by Purdue University’s Skill Learning and Performance Lab (hhs.purdue.edu), the Case Western Reserve University news release (case.edu) and the APS press release (psychologicalscience.org).

summary: A sport-specific meta-analysis of the relationship between deliberate practice and performance. Practice accounted for about 18% of the variance in sports performance overall, and for only about 1% among elite-level athletes. The authors argue that practice matters but that other factors must explain most differences, especially at the top. An author copy is hosted by a university lab page.
arguments: Across sports, accumulated deliberate practice explains a meaningful but minority share of performance differences.
Among elite athletes, differences in accumulated practice explain almost none of the differences in performance.
Expertise research in sport should test additional factors rather than assume practice is sufficient.
design: Meta-analysis of sport studies relating accumulated deliberate practice to performance, with moderator analyses by skill level.
strengths: Focused on sport, where deliberate-practice claims are most often applied; analyzes skill level as a moderator.
limitations: Relies on primary studies’ retrospective practice estimates; the elite-level result is expected partly because of range restriction (elite athletes all practice a great deal), which limits what it says about the value of practice for any individual.
contested: Disputed by Ericsson and colleagues on definitional grounds (R-ericsson-2019-deliberate).
generalizability: Directly applicable to athlete development. It informs talent identification more than it informs practice design.
relevance: The figure you need when someone argues that development outcomes are simply a matter of more reps.

title: The Role of Deliberate Practice in Expert Performance: Revisiting Ericsson, Krampe & Tesch-Römer (1993)
license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, article number and publication date matched on pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (PMC6731745) and the Purdue University lab page (hhs.purdue.edu); data deposit matched on datadryad.org. The article DOI was not shown in results and is omitted.

summary: A replication of the classic violin study behind deliberate-practice theory. Violinists at three skill levels gave practice estimates and rated practice activities. The authors did not reproduce the original core finding that accumulated deliberate practice corresponded to each skill level; the relationship they found was substantial but considerably smaller than in the original. Full text and data are openly available.
arguments: The strongest original evidence for deliberate-practice theory did not fully replicate.
Practice still showed a substantial relationship with skill, but smaller than first reported.
Participants rated teacher-designed practice as less relevant to improvement than practice alone, which bears on how deliberate practice is defined.
design: Close replication of the 1993 violinist comparison: skill groups, retrospective practice estimates and activity ratings; data posted publicly.
strengths: Direct replication with open data; tests the founding claim rather than a reinterpretation.
limitations: Small sample, as in the original; still relies on retrospective estimates and group comparisons; one domain.
contested: Part of an ongoing exchange with Ericsson and colleagues about definitions and measurement (R-ericsson-2019-deliberate).
generalizability: A caution about building development philosophies on a single influential study.
relevance: A model of how a responsible field revisits its own foundations — and a reminder to check whether a famous finding has been replicated.

title: Deliberate Practice and Proposed Limits on the Effects of Practice on the Acquisition of Expert Performance
license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Authors, journal, volume, article number, date and DOI matched on frontiersin.org, pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (PMC6824411) and doaj.org; the reanalysis figures matched in the abstract text shown in results. Only the main title was confirmed; any subtitle is omitted.

summary: Ericsson’s reply to the meta-analytic critiques. The authors argue that the meta-analyses counted structured practice in general rather than deliberate practice as originally defined (individualized training designed by a teacher to improve specific aspects of performance). Reanalyzing only studies that match the original definition, they report that practice explained considerably more variance — figures of 29% and, after correcting for measurement attenuation, 61%. They recommend measuring the quality of practice, not only its duration.
arguments: Definitions matter: averaging across loosely defined practice underestimates the effect of deliberate practice.
Studies that match the original definition show larger relationships with performance.
Future research should measure concentration, analysis and problem solving during practice, not just hours.
design: Critical review and reanalysis of a subset of studies selected by the original definition of deliberate practice.
strengths: Clarifies the theory’s definition; makes a fair point that hours are a crude proxy for practice quality.
limitations: Written by the theory’s originator; the reanalysis rests on a small, selected set of studies; corrections for attenuation can inflate estimates when reliability is uncertain.
contested: Responds to R-macnamara-2014-deliberate and R-macnamara-2016-relationship; the replication R-macnamara-2019-role bears on the same question.
generalizability: The emphasis on practice quality is directly useful to coaches; the larger variance estimates should be held loosely until independent tests confirm them.
relevance: Lets you see the strongest version of the other side of the debate, which is what an executive must do before deciding.

title: Contextual Interference Effects on the Acquisition, Retention, and Transfer of a Motor Skill
publication: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Learning and Memory, 5(2), 179–187
license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages and year matched on the swov.nl library record and a scan of the original article; design and findings matched in later reviews indexed on pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov. The DOI was not shown in results and is omitted.

summary: The experiment that launched contextual-interference research. Participants learned three movement patterns (knocking down barriers in set sequences) either in blocks or in a random order. Blocked practice produced better performance during acquisition, but random practice produced better retention, especially when retention was tested in a random order, and better transfer, especially to the most complex transfer task.
arguments: Practicing several skills in a random order makes practice harder and in-session performance worse.
The same random schedule produced better retention and transfer than blocked practice.
The best acquisition schedule and the best learning schedule can be opposites.
design: Laboratory experiment: blocked versus random practice of three barrier knock-down movement patterns; retention after 10 minutes or 10 days under blocked and random test orders; transfer tasks of differing complexity.
strengths: Elegant design separating acquisition, retention and transfer; launched a large literature.
limitations: Simple laboratory movements, university participants, short training; whether the effect holds for complex sport skills in real practice is a separate question.
contested: The laboratory effect is well reproduced; applied-setting effects are smaller and contested (R-czyz-2024-effect, R-ammar-2023-myth).
generalizability: Strong as a demonstration of the learning–performance distinction in motor skills; modest and uncertain as a prescription for sport practice.
relevance: The classic you will see cited to justify random practice; knowing exactly what it did and did not test protects you from over-reading it.

title: The Effect of Contextual Interference on Transfer in Motor Learning: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, article number, publication date (14 August 2024) and DOI matched on frontiersin.org and pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (PMC11349744); effect sizes matched in the abstract text shown in results.

summary: A meta-analysis of 34 studies on whether high contextual interference (random practice) improves transfer of motor skills. Overall, random practice was favored with a medium effect (SMD = 0.55). In laboratory studies the effect was medium and statistically significant (SMD = 0.75); in applied settings it was small and not statistically significant (SMD = 0.34); in young participants it was negligible (SMD = 0.12). A companion paper by the same group reports a retention benefit.
arguments: Random practice tends to improve transfer of motor skills on average.
The effect is clearer in laboratory tasks than in applied sport and physical-education settings.
Age and setting moderate the effect, so a single prescription for all learners is not justified.
design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of experiments comparing high and low contextual interference with a transfer test; subgroup analyses by setting and age.
strengths: Recent, focused on transfer (the outcome coaches care about), and reports the laboratory–applied gap explicitly.
limitations: Applied studies are fewer and noisier, so the applied estimate is imprecise; the authors favor the contextual-interference hypothesis, while other recent meta-analyses read the evidence more skeptically.
contested: Read alongside R-ammar-2023-myth, which finds little support for applied benefits; the two groups have exchanged published critiques.
generalizability: The most relevant single estimate for sport: expect a smaller and less certain benefit in real practice than in laboratory demonstrations.
relevance: Shows exactly where a famous laboratory effect becomes uncertain — at the point where you would apply it.

title: The Myth of Contextual Interference Learning Benefit in Sports Practice: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, journal, volume, year (May 2023) and author surnames matched in a library catalogue record (katalog.lib.cas.cz) and search-result summaries; the URL is built from the Elsevier article identifier shown in that catalogue record. Given names and DOI were not confirmed and are omitted.

summary: A systematic review and meta-analysis, with meta-regression, of contextual-interference studies in sport practice. The authors report little evidence that the contextual-interference benefit generalizes to applied physical-education and sport settings and argue that the benefit has been overstated. The same group later published a further critical review and an exchange with proponents.
arguments: Laboratory demonstrations of contextual interference do not reliably translate into benefits in sport practice.
Coaching recommendations based on the effect have outrun the applied evidence.
Practice design should not rest on a single scheduling principle.
design: Systematic review and meta-analysis with meta-regression of contextual-interference studies in applied sport and physical-education settings.
strengths: Focuses on applied settings, where the decision is actually made; part of a transparent published exchange.
limitations: Applied studies vary widely in skills, durations and tests; conclusions depend on inclusion choices that proponents dispute. Details beyond the abstract-level description were not confirmed for this record.
contested: Directly opposed in its reading of the evidence by R-czyz-2024-effect.
generalizability: Directly about sport practice. Treat it as the skeptical side of a live debate, not as settled.
relevance: The counterweight you need before mandating random practice across a development system.

title: Superiority of External Attentional Focus for Motor Performance and Learning: Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses
license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author surnames, journal, volume, issue, pages and DOI matched on digitalscholarship.unlv.edu and pure.psu.edu; study counts and effect sizes matched in the abstract text shown in results. The first author’s full name matched; other given names are as commonly listed.

summary: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses comparing an external focus of attention (on the movement’s effect, such as the target or the implement) with an internal focus (on body movements). Pooling 73 studies for performance and 40 for learning, the authors report advantages for an external focus: Hedges’ g of about 0.26 for performance, 0.58 for retention and 0.58 for transfer, with no significant moderation by age, health status or skill level.
arguments: Directing attention to the intended movement effect rather than to body parts improves performance and learning on average.
The benefit appeared across ages, health conditions and skill levels in the included studies.
Electromyography studies suggested more efficient muscular activity under an external focus, and a more distant external focus did better than a near one.
design: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses: 73 studies (1,824 participants) for performance and 40 studies (1,274 participants) for retention and transfer; subsets of 12 electromyography studies and 9 studies of distance of focus.
strengths: Large, systematic synthesis of a well-known coaching principle.
limitations: Many small studies; authors include the principle’s leading proponent; a later reanalysis argues that publication bias explains most of the effect.
contested: Reanalysis with bias-correction methods finds effects near zero (R-mckay-2024-reporting).
generalizability: Plausible and cheap to apply in coaching language; the size of the benefit in real sport settings is uncertain.
relevance: The best case for one of the most widely taught coaching principles — read it with its critique.

title: Reporting Bias, Not External Focus: A Robust Bayesian Meta-Analysis and Systematic Review of the External Focus of Attention Literature
license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Author surnames, journal, volume, issue, pages and DOI matched on experts.mcmaster.ca; findings matched in the abstract shown on x-mol.com. Title wording differs between listings (preprint and published versions), and given names were not confirmed and are omitted.

summary: A reanalysis of the external-focus literature using robust Bayesian meta-analysis, which models several forms of publication bias. The authors found moderate to strong evidence of publication bias in every analysis. After correction, estimated effects were near zero — about g = 0.01 for performance, 0.15 for retention and 0.09 for transfer — and Bayes factors favored the null. They conclude that an external-focus advantage has not been established.
arguments: The external-focus literature shows strong signs that small studies with positive results were more likely to be published.
Once bias is modeled, the evidence favors little or no average benefit.
A widely taught coaching principle can rest on a literature that looks stronger than it is.
design: Robust Bayesian meta-analysis and systematic review of external- versus internal-focus studies, modeling multiple publication-bias scenarios.
strengths: Uses modern bias-correction methods; transparent about assumptions; addresses the exact literature coaches rely on.
limitations: Bias-correction methods rest on their own assumptions and can understate true effects; absence of evidence for an average benefit is not proof that no learner benefits.
contested: Directly contradicts the conclusion of R-chua-2021-superiority.
generalizability: A general lesson for sport science: small-sample literatures can produce confident principles that shrink under scrutiny.
relevance: Shows you how to hold a coaching principle at the right level of confidence when the evidence base is contested.

title: Learning Styles: Concepts and Evidence
publication: Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 9(3), 105–119
license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, PSPI 9(3) 105–119, year (December 2008 issue) and DOI matched on digitalcommons.usf.edu; some sources give 2009 (DOI registration year).

summary: A review of the claim that instruction should be matched to each learner’s preferred learning style. The authors specify the kind of experiment needed to support the matching claim — learners classified by style, randomly assigned to matched or mismatched instruction, with a crossover interaction on a common test — and conclude that well-designed tests of this kind were virtually absent and that those that existed did not support the claim.
arguments: People do have preferences about how information is presented; preference is not the same as benefit.
Supporting the matching hypothesis requires a crossover interaction, not just a difference between groups.
The authors judged that the evidence did not justify spending resources on style assessment and matched instruction.
design: Critical review defining the evidential standard for the learning-styles matching hypothesis and evaluating the literature against it.
strengths: Clear statement of what evidence would be needed; widely cited in education policy debates.
limitations: A review of evidence available at the time; it does not claim that all individual differences are irrelevant to instruction.
contested: The conclusion is broadly accepted among learning scientists; belief in learning styles remains common among practitioners.
generalizability: Applies to education, corporate training and coaching: assessing a “style” and matching instruction to it is not a supported basis for practice design.
relevance: A model of how to test a plausible, popular idea — and a myth you will meet in coaching education and vendor pitches.

title: Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later
license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, Educational Psychology Review 31(2) 261–292, year and DOI matched on cris.maastrichtuniversity.nl and deutsche-digitale-bibliothek.de.

summary: A twenty-year update of cognitive load theory by its principal authors. Learning complex material is constrained by a limited working memory and enabled by a vast long-term memory that stores organized knowledge (schemas). Instruction should manage the load imposed by the material and avoid load created by poor presentation. The review discusses effects such as the benefit of worked examples for novices and the expertise reversal effect, in which methods that help novices become redundant or harmful for more expert learners.
arguments: Working memory is severely limited for new information; long-term knowledge effectively expands it for familiar material.
Instruction should reduce extraneous load (load created by presentation) so that capacity is available for the task itself.
The best instructional method depends on the learner’s expertise: guidance that helps novices can hinder experts.
design: Theoretical review summarizing a research program of experiments on instructional design.
strengths: Coherent theory linked to many controlled experiments; explicit about how instructional effects depend on expertise.
limitations: Written by the theory’s founders; cognitive load is difficult to measure directly and is often assessed by self-rated mental effort; most research concerns academic and technical material rather than motor skills.
generalizability: Useful for designing how coaches explain, demonstrate and sequence information, and for onboarding in any knowledge-heavy role. Application to motor skills is by analogy and should be tested.
relevance: Explains why the coach who says ten things after every repetition usually helps less than the coach who says one.

title: Does Far Transfer Exist? Negative Evidence From Chess, Music, and Working Memory Training
license: Creative Commons Attribution licence (per PMC and university repository listings). Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, Current Directions in Psychological Science 26(6) 515–520, year and DOI matched on pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (PMID 29276344) and journals.sagepub.com; open-access copy in PMC (PMC5724589).

summary: A short review of meta-analytic evidence on far transfer — whether training in one domain improves general cognitive or academic abilities in unrelated domains. Drawing on meta-analyses of chess instruction, music training and working-memory training, the authors conclude that far transfer is rare and that apparent benefits tend to shrink as study quality improves.
arguments: Skills tend to be specific to the domain in which they are practiced.
Reported far-transfer effects are small and decrease in better-controlled studies.
Training programs should target the skills that matter directly rather than rely on general transfer.
design: Brief review of the authors’ and others’ meta-analyses of chess, music and working-memory training.
strengths: Concise synthesis across three popular training domains; attends to study quality.
limitations: Concerns cognitive and academic outcomes; does not address near transfer within a sport or profession, where transfer is more plausible.
generalizability: Supports a strong default: expect skills to transfer only to tasks that share their underlying demands.
relevance: A useful corrective when someone claims a drill, game or app builds a general capacity that will show up elsewhere.

title: The Effects of Feedback Interventions on Performance: A Historical Review, a Meta-Analysis, and a Preliminary Feedback Intervention Theory
license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, Psychological Bulletin 119(2) 254–284 and year matched on cris.huji.ac.il and scholars.huji.ac.il; the DOI did not appear in two searches and was removed.

summary: A historical review and meta-analysis of feedback interventions. Feedback improved performance on average, but a large share of interventions reduced performance. The authors propose feedback intervention theory: feedback works by directing attention, and it helps less, or harms, when it draws attention away from the task toward the self.
arguments: Feedback interventions have a positive average effect but highly variable results.
A substantial share of feedback interventions lowered performance.
Feedback that directs attention to the self (praise or criticism of the person) tends to weaken effects; feedback about the task and how to improve it tends to help.
design: Meta-analysis of feedback-intervention studies with a control condition, plus a theoretical synthesis.
strengths: Seminal; the variability finding has shaped feedback research for three decades.
limitations: Many included studies were laboratory tasks; workplace coaching conversations are richer than the interventions coded.
generalizability: The attention mechanism is plausible across settings; precise effect sizes should not be transferred to managerial conversations.
relevance: The strongest single correction to the belief that more feedback is always better.
